Summary of Economic Metrics for Chiller-Based and GeoSWAC Systems ............................... 31 vii This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 1 Introduction Puerto Rico, a U.S. territory situated roughly 1,600 km (1,000 miles) southeast of Miami, sits in the direct path of powerful Atlantic hurricanes. The island’s exposure to warm ocean waters, high humidity, and prevailing wind patterns makes it especially susceptible to tropical storms that damage critical infrastructure. This vulnerability is compounded by a heavy reliance on expensive imported energy. The devastating impact of Hurricane Maria in 2017 underscored these risks. Making landfall as a Category 4 storm and briefly reaching Category 5 intensity, Maria triggered the longest blackout in U.S. history, lasting nearly a year for some communities in Puerto Rico, and was linked to thousands of fatalities (Santos-Burgoa et al. 2018; Kishore et al. 2018). Puerto Rico experiences consistently high temperatures and humidity throughout the year, creating a strong and growing demand for cooling, particularly for air conditioning in residential, commercial, and public buildings. Peak electricity demand is heavily influenced by cooling needs, especially during the hot summer months and periods of heat waves. Most buildings on the island are not designed with passive cooling in mind and rely heavily on air-conditioning systems. This has led to a significant increase in energy consumption, especially during midday and early evening hours. The island’s aging electrical grid and dependence on expensive imported fuels makes meeting increased electricity demand costly and leaves the island vulnerable to power disruptions, especially during hurricanes and other extreme weather events (Pokhrel et al. 2019; Baggu et al. 2024). Moreover, rising urbanization is expected to significantly increase cooling demand in the coming decades, placing additional strain on existing infrastructure. The adoption of more efficient cooling technologies is essential to address these challenges. Ongoing efforts are focused on improving energy efficiency and promoting alternative energy sources for cooling, aligning with Puerto Rico’s broader goals for energy flexibility. This study explores a novel concept termed geologic seawater air conditioning (GeoSWAC) (Oh et al. 2025a). The concept is inspired by seawater air conditioning (SWAC), which has emerged as a potential alternative for reducing reliance on conventional, electricity-intensive cooling systems in tropical coastal regions (Makai Ocean Engineering 2008; Lilley et al. 2015; Hunt et al. 2019, 2022).
